 District 7 Fresno City Council candidates make final push as Election Day nears 
 The two candidates competing for an open Fresno City Council District 7 seat are spending their final weekend focused on one goal: turnout. By Grant Johnson Monday, November 2, 2026 1:33PM Share FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- With Election Day less than 48 hours away, the two candidates competing for an open Fresno City Council District 7 seat are spending their final weekend focused on one goal: turnout.
 Only about 20 votes separated the candidates in June's primary election, making it the closest Fresno City Council race on the ballot.
 Now, attorney Nav Gurm and community organizer Ariana Martinez Lott are making their closing arguments directly to voters across the district before Tuesday's runoff.
 Gurm, an attorney and former staffer for Councilmember Nelson Esparza, spent part of Sunday canvassing east central Fresno, where he has been knocking on doors since launching his campaign in January 2025.
 "It's really having conversations with your own neighbors. I try not to make it too sales-pitchy," Gurm said.
 Gurm cast his ballot Sunday at Melody Park.
 "I just finished voting. It was an honor to vote for myself for the second time. So just humbled to be here and take part in our great democracy," he said.
 Gurm finished first in the June primary but did not receive a majority of votes needed to avoid a runoff. As Election Day approaches, he said his campaign's strategy has evolved from persuasion to turnout.
 "We've made a strong case for ourselves. We were thankful to finish first in the primary and hoping to finish strong on Tuesday," Gurm said. "One thing we've been doing in the past week or two is really shifting our messaging more from persuasion to encourage people to vote."
 Across the district, Martinez Lott began Saturday by dispatching volunteers to canvass neighborhoods.
 "Really appreciate you being willing to volunteer your time to be out here," she told supporters. "Thank you for helping us make that big final push."
 Martinez Lott, a community organizer and former staffer for Councilmember Miguel Arias, said her campaign has centered on relationships with residents and concerns about government accountability.
 "One of the biggest things that I've heard from residents at the doors is that, hey, we believe that you're doing this for the right reasons, but we just want to make sure that you're actually going to show up after election season. Because what residents oftentimes see is candidates show up only during election season," she said.

 She also said voters are looking for candidates who connect campaign promises to everyday concerns.
 "What we oftentimes hear during campaign seasons is big promises from candidates. But if those promises are not directly connected to people's everyday experiences, they stay as just that: promises," Martinez Lott said.
 As the campaign enters its final days, Martinez Lott urged residents who have not yet voted to participate.
 "I know that we're living in a time where we're losing faith in government, but at the end of the day, this is a way that we can continue to put our values into action. It is not too late if somebody hasn't voted. Now is the time," she said.
 The District 7 contest appears on a lengthy ballot that also includes 14 statewide propositions and two countywide measures.
 Fresno County Registrar of Voters James Kus said the length of this year's ballot is expected to slow tabulation compared with shorter elections.
 Kus said election officials expect to release the first batch of results shortly after 8 p.m. on election night, with those initial numbers consisting of vote-by-mail ballots already received.
 He also encouraged voters not to wait until Election Day to return their ballots.
 "Unfortunately, Fresno County is pretty bad at this, but California in general has a lot of voters that wait until Election Day either to vote in person or to drop off their vote by mail ballot," Kus said.
 "We received 50% of all vote by mail ballots on Election Day, and that creates an incredible bottleneck. If we were receiving 15 or 20,000 per day for the 10 days before Election Day, we'd be all caught up and there'd be no problem. But instead, we get 120 or 150,000 on one day."
 Kus added, "I really want to encourage anyone who wants it, who can, to vote early, whether it be by vote by mail or in person. There will absolutely be lines on Election Day."
 Voters who still have their ballots can return them at any Fresno County vote center or official county drop box. Vote centers are scheduled to reopen at 9 a.m. Monday ahead of Election Day.
